notes.b: Lipids (fats and oils) do far more in the body than provide energy. Each function below follows from where fat sits in the body or what it does as it passes through the digestive system.
points: Lipids are a concentrated source of energy, supplying the body with more energy per gram than carbohydrate or protein, so a small amount of fat gives a lot of energy.
Excess energy from any food is stored as adipose tissue (the body's stored fat), which is a reserve of energy for when food intake is low.
Adipose tissue lies under the skin and insulates the body against heat loss, which helps to keep body temperature constant.
Adipose tissue around organs such as the kidneys and heart cushions them against knocks and pressure, and holds them in place.
Lipids slow the emptying of the stomach, which helps to delay hunger, so meals containing fat are more satisfying.
notes.tip: Name two or three functions and give a reason for each; for example, adipose tissue insulates because it reduces heat loss. Name a dietary source with a function if asked. Do not call fat the main source of energy: carbohydrates are the body's main energy source and fat is the concentrated one.

notes.h: Lipids as carriers, building material and flavour
notes.b: Beyond energy and body protection, lipids carry nutrients, build cell structures and affect how food tastes.
points: Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K and help the body absorb them, because these vitamins dissolve in fat and not in water. Dairy fat, oily fish and egg yolk supply them.
Lipids are a source of essential fatty acids, the fatty acids the body cannot make for itself and must get from food.
Phospholipids (fat-like lipids containing phosphorus) and cholesterol form part of the structure of every cell membrane, the thin layer around each cell.
Fat also adds flavour and a smooth texture to food, although this is a cooking benefit and not a biological function.
Digestion link: the enzyme lipase digests triglycerides (the main fats in food) to fatty acids and glycerol, and any excess is stored as adipose tissue.

notes.b: Cholesterol is a lipid that is often blamed for heart disease, yet the body needs it. It is different from the saturated fat in food, and students often confuse the two.
points: Cholesterol is a fat-like substance called a sterol, found only in animal foods such as egg yolk, offal (liver and kidney), meat, butter, cream, cheese, prawns and other shellfish. Plant foods contain none.
The liver makes cholesterol itself, in fact most of what the body has, so the amount eaten has less effect on blood cholesterol than the saturated fat in the diet.
Saturated fat in the diet raises blood LDL cholesterol more than dietary cholesterol does. A plant oil such as coconut oil is cholesterol-free but can still be high in saturated fat.

The body uses cholesterol to make cell membranes, bile salts that emulsify fat (break it into tiny droplets) for digestion, and steroid hormones such as oestrogen, progesterone, testosterone and cortisol.
Vitamin D is made in the skin from a derivative of cholesterol.

Too much cholesterol in the blood, especially LDL, builds up on artery walls and narrows them, which increases the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) and stroke. It is also a main constituent of most gallstones.

To lower blood cholesterol, eat less saturated and trans fat and more unsaturated fat, oily fish, oats, pulses, fruit and vegetables (their fibre helps). Keep to a healthy weight, be active and do not smoke.
Functional spreads containing plant stanols or sterols also help to lower blood cholesterol.
notes.tip: For a cholesterol question, give a definition, the source (animal foods only), the uses, the health risk and how to lower it. 'A high intake of saturated fat leads to low cholesterol' is false.

notes.h: Health effects of a diet high in saturated fat
notes.b: Foods high in saturated fat are energy-dense and raise blood LDL cholesterol. A diet high in them over years raises the risk of several diseases, and each has its own mechanism.
points: Obesity: saturated-fat foods are energy-dense, and surplus energy from them is stored as adipose tissue, which can lead to obesity.

Coronary heart disease and high blood pressure: raised LDL cholesterol narrows the arteries (atherosclerosis), increasing the risk of coronary heart disease, high blood pressure (hypertension) and stroke.
Type 2 diabetes: excess body fat reduces the effectiveness of insulin (the hormone that controls blood sugar), which is called insulin resistance, so the risk of Type 2 diabetes increases.
Gallstones: cholesterol is a main component of gallstones, which can form in the gall bladder.
Varicose veins and infertility are also linked to a high-fat diet; the first four effects carry the most weight.
Lifestyle changes recommended for someone at risk of CHD: a low-fat, low-cholesterol, low-salt diet; losing weight; not smoking; limiting alcohol; exercise; and managing stress.

Irish healthy eating guidelines from the Department of Health advise replacing saturated fats with unsaturated (mono- and polyunsaturated) fats and using fats and oils in small amounts, which is the fats, spreads and oils shelf of the Food Pyramid.
Other advice: choose lean meat and low-fat dairy, and grill, steam or bake instead of frying. Saturated fat should supply less than 10% of daily energy (HSE and Department of Health guidelines).
notes.tip: Give each effect with its mechanism: adipose tissue for obesity, LDL narrowing arteries for heart disease and high blood pressure, and insulin working less well for Type 2 diabetes. Naming a disease without the mechanism loses marks.

notes.b: Energy is measured in kilojoules (kJ) or kilocalories (kcal). Fat has the highest energy value per gram of the three nutrients, which is why fatty foods are so energy-dense.
points: Fat provides 37 kJ or 9 kcal of energy per gram, which is more than twice the energy per gram of carbohydrate or protein. The true/false statement that 1 gram of fat provides 20 kilocalories is false.
Carbohydrate provides 16 kJ or 3.75 kcal per gram; protein provides 17 kJ or 4 kcal per gram; alcohol provides 29 kJ or 7 kcal per gram.
Energy from fat is calculated by multiplying the grams of fat by 37 kJ, or by 9 kcal.
Worked example (sample data): 20 g of fat gives 20 × 37 = 740 kJ, or 20 × 9 = 180 kcal.

A large part of the energy in the average Irish diet comes from fat, much of it hidden in processed and convenience foods, meat products, dairy, cakes, pastries, biscuits, chocolate, fried foods and takeaways, and much of that is saturated.

Guidance is to reduce total fat, especially saturated and trans fat, replacing them with unsaturated fat and complex carbohydrate. Over-consumption of fat leads to obesity because fat is energy-dense and stores readily.
notes.tip: Learn 37 kJ or 9 kcal per gram: fat is not 4 kcal and not 20 kcal. In a data question, multiply the grams of fat by 37 or by 9, and show the working. Three ways to cut fat intake: choose lean meat, use low-fat dairy and grill instead of frying.

keyTerms.definition: Body fat stored under the skin and around organs, which provides energy, insulation and cushioning.
A lipid containing phosphorus that forms the structure of cell membranes.
A sterol found in animal foods that the body needs for cell membranes, bile salts and hormones.
A vitamin, such as A, D, E or K, that dissolves in fat and is carried by lipids in the body.
The amount of energy a food provides per gram, which is highest for fat.
A unit of energy used in food labelling, equal to 1000 joules.
A unit of energy, also called a Calorie, commonly used on food labels, equal to 4.184 kJ.
The feeling of fullness that reduces hunger and stops eating.
A hardened deposit that can form in the gall bladder from cholesterol and bile.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which lipids protect or insulate the body, and explain how each one works.
questions.model: Insulation: adipose tissue under the skin traps body heat and reduces heat loss to the environment. Protection: a layer of adipose tissue around organs such as the kidneys cushions them against knocks and pressure. Award one mark for each way named and one for each correct explanation, up to 6 in total.

questions.prompt: Compare the energy value of lipids with that of carbohydrate and protein, then discuss how a diet high in saturated fat can affect health.
questions.model: Fat provides 37 kJ or 9 kcal per gram, carbohydrate 16 kJ or 3.75 kcal per gram and protein 17 kJ or 4 kcal per gram, so fat is the most energy-dense nutrient. Excess energy from fat is stored as adipose tissue, which can lead to obesity. Saturated fat raises LDL cholesterol, which deposits cholesterol on artery walls, increasing the risk of coronary heart disease and high blood pressure. Excess body fat reduces the effectiveness of insulin, increasing the risk of Type 2 diabetes. Cholesterol is a main component of gallstones. Irish healthy eating guidelines from the Department of Health advise replacing saturated fats with unsaturated fats.
